report.source_text: A few days later, however, an acute confusional state prompted brain MRI. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging revealed symmetrical hyperintensities strictly limited to the subcortical precentral gyrus (Fig. 1a). Correspondingly, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed signal hyperintensity (Fig. 1b), along with normal ADC and without any contrast enhancement. Six days before transplant, the patient had received cranial MRI without any pathological finding. Thus, tetraplegia was attributable to new symmetrical CNS lesions.

CSF analysis would be critical to evaluate for viral infection and exclude other etiologies.

report.source_text: Accordingly, intravenous ganciclovir treatment (5 mg per kg per day over two weeks) was initiated. Over the following three weeks, serum PCR for CMV turned negative. Tetraparesis slowly improved, with still moderate pareses of the upper (between MRC 3 and 4), but severe pareses of the lower (between MRC 1 and 2) extremities at neurological reassessment four weeks after symptom onset. Unfortunately, in the further course the patient developed a septic syndrome, most likely owing to a pulmonary focus, and exspired due to septic multiple organ failure. Autopsy was prohibited.
report.temporal_cue: over the following three weeks and four weeks after symptom onset

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 51-year-old patient six weeks post stem cell transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, receiving strong immunosuppression with cyclosporine A and mycophenolate mofetil, developed high-grade pure motor flaccid tetraparesis within days. Brain MRI revealed new symmetrical subcortical FLAIR hyperintensities strictly limited to the precentral gyrus with DWI hyperintensity and normal ADC, without contrast enhancement, representing new lesions compared to pre-transplant imaging. CSF analysis demonstrated elevated protein (56.2 mg/dl) and albumin (50.9 mg/dl) with normal cell count (1 leukocyte/mm3) and negative PCR for multiple neurotropic viruses and bacterial DNA. Serum CMV PCR showed progressively increasing viral load up to 8,600 copies/ml starting shortly before neurological symptom onset. Intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg/day for two weeks) was initiated, resulting in clearance of CMV viremia over three weeks and slow clinical improvement in tetraparesis (upper extremities MRC 3-4, lower extremities MRC 1-2 at four weeks). The patient subsequently expired from septic multiple organ failure.
